title: Retinoblastoma: Genetics, Heritage & Risk Dynamics
summary: A comprehensive deep-dive into the hereditary landscape of RB1 mutations, focusing on the clinical application of Knudson’s Two-Hit Hypothesis, penetrance statistics, and evidence-based screening protocols for at-risk offspring and siblings.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, arising from neuroepithelial cells (retinoblasts) in the developing retina. It is fundamentally a disease of the cell cycle, caused by the biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 13q14. Understanding heritage is critical because germline mutations predispose individuals not only to bilateral ocular tumors but also to primitive neuroectodermal tumors (trilateral RB) and secondary non-ocular malignancies later in life.

sections.title: Etiology: The RB1 Gene
content: Locus: Chromosome 13q14.2
Function: Encodes pRb protein, which regulates the G1 to S phase transition in the cell cycle.
Mechanism: pRb binds to E2F transcription factors, inhibiting DNA synthesis.
Inactivation: Phosphorylation by Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) releases E2F, allowing cell cycle progression.

sections.title: Knudson’s Two-Hit Hypothesis
content: Step 1: The First Hit — In heritable RB, this is a germline mutation (present in all cells). In sporadic RB, this is a somatic mutation in a single retinal cell.
Step 2: The Second Hit — A second event (mutation, deletion, or methylation) inactivates the remaining wild-type allele in a precursor retinoblast.
Step 3: Malignant Transformation — Loss of both functional RB1 alleles leads to uncontrolled proliferation and tumor formation.

Step 4: Clinical Result — Germline 'hits' often lead to multifocal/bilateral disease because only one more hit is needed in any cell. Somatic 'hits' require two rare events in the same cell, leading to unifocal disease.

sections.title: Hereditary Risk: Offspring of a Survivor
Hereditary Risk: Siblings of an Affected Child

branches: Penetrance: ~90% (Not everyone with the mutation gets a tumor)
Variable Expressivity: Severity differs between individuals
Retinoma: Benign, arrested version of RB
Low-Penetrance Phenotypes: Associated with specific missense mutations

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Trilateral Retinoblastoma: Pineoblastoma or parasellar tumor in a germline patient.
Orbital Extension: Proptosis or extraocular mass (High mortality).
Glaucoma in a child: Neovascularization of the iris (NVI) is common in advanced RB.
Pseudohypopyon: Tumor seeds in the anterior chamber mimicking inflammation.

sections.title: Screening Protocol for At-Risk Relatives
content: Birth to 3 Months: Examination every 3-4 weeks (EUA if necessary).
3 Months to 1 Year: Examination every 6-8 weeks.
1 Year to 3 Years: Examination every 3-4 months.
3 Years to 5 Years: Examination every 6 months.
After Age 5: Annual exams indefinitely (risk of retinoma/secondary tumors).

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Leukocoria (60%): 'White pupil' or 'cat's eye reflex'.
Strabismus (20%): Due to macular involvement.
Secondary Glaucoma: Often with buphthalmos.
Atypical: Vitreous seeds mimicking endophthalmitis.
Hyphaema or Anterior Chamber seeds.
Retinal Detachment: Usually exudative.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Chemoreduction: Vincristine, Etoposide, Carboplatin (VEC protocol) to shrink tumors.
Intra-arterial Chemotherapy (IAC): Melphalan delivered via ophthalmic artery (Standard for Groups B-D).
Intravitreal Chemotherapy: For active vitreous seeds.
Local Therapy: Cryotherapy (for peripheral) or Laser Photocoagulation/TTT (for posterior).
Enucleation: For Group E eyes or failed conservative therapy (Long optic nerve stump required).
Plaque Brachytherapy: For salvage of solitary, medium-sized tumors.

content.explanation: 13q14 (Locus), Quiescent (pRb state in G0), Vincristine-Etoposide-Carboplatin (Standard Chemo).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Bilateral RB is ALWAYS germline.
Unilateral RB with multiple foci is ALWAYS germline.
Genetic testing of the tumor (if enucleated) is superior to blood testing alone.
Avoid external beam radiation (EBRT) in germline patients due to high risk of secondary sarcomas.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Liquid Biopsy
content: Aqueous Humor Analysis: Detection of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in the aqueous humor allows for genetic profiling without biopsy (biopsy is contraindicated due to seeding risk).
Copy Number Variation (CNV): Gains in 1q, 6p, and losses in 16q are predictive of treatment response.
Targeted Therapy: Use of MDM2/MDMX inhibitors in RB1-wildtype (MYCN amplified) cases.
